19132-banbury-chap-books-and-nursery-toy:
This study of Banbury chap books and nursery toy book literature covers the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. It reproduces woodcuts by Bewick, Blake, Cruikshank, and others, and traces small cheap books sold for children, from Goody Two Shoes to the Cries of York. More than eight hundred small pictures are noted in the text.

The author follows collections formed for the South Kensington Museum and notes how prices rose as such little books grew rare. Charles Knight's love for Newbury's gilt-bound volumes gets a fond mention. Readers get a rich picture book history of early children's print, its makers, and its collectors.
26073-the-metamorphoses-of-ovid-books-vi:
Ovid's Metamorphoses continues here in its second half, Books VIII through XV, in Henry T. Riley's 1851 translation as reprinted by George Bell in 1893. A synoptical view lists the chief transformations, and each fable carries the line numbers of the Latin poem, with notes and single Greek words kept in the text.

The tales run from gods and heroes to birds and beasts. One tale tells of Ceyx, whose grieving wife takes wing as a bird and skims the water to reach his lifeless body. Translator's additions appear in braces, and italics in the notes follow the usual marks. The book closes Ovid's chain of changes, where human sorrow and divine power meet in new shapes.
54545-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for June 1913, volume eighty-six, number two, is a travel number. A painting of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia by Guerin fronts the issue. Hesse-Wartegg writes on the Great Saint Bernard, with pictures by Castaigne. Frances Little treats the training of a Japanese child from photographs. The Century's after-the-war series takes another view of the Hayes-Tilden contest, and Colonel Watterson replies to Senator Edmunds in the same number.

Joseph Pennell contributes six lithographs of the Grand Canyon drawn from nature. Hichens skirts the Balkan peninsula at Delphi and Olympia; Moser nooses wild elephants; John Quincy Adams's letters from Russia appear with an introduction by his grandson. Cable's Belles Demoiselles Plantation represents the noteworthy stories of the last generation. Burnett's T Tembarom runs as a serial. Editorials treat privacy, government, and the two-billion-dollar Congress.
56839-the-century-illustrated-monthly-ma:
The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine for July 1913 is volume eighty-six, number three, a fiction number. Its contents open with how Beelzebub came to the convent, by Ethel Watts Mumford, with a picture by Wyeth. Millet's return to his old home, by Truman Bartlett, follows, with pictures from pastels by Millet. The man who did not go to heaven on Tuesday, by Ellis Parker Butler, comes next.

The borrowed lover, by Tooker, and memories of Frederic Remington, by Augustus Thomas, fill the next pages. The American spinster is treated by Agnes Repplier. The coming sneeze, by Harry Stillwell Edwards, and a Balkan travel piece by Robert Hichens follow. Camilla's first affair, by Gertrude Hall, and Tembarom, by Frances Hodgson Burnett, stand among the fiction. A life of St Elizabeth of Hungary and a piece on the return to hard money close the contents.
73192-the-court-of-louis-xv:
The Court of Louis XV belongs to a series on famous women of the French court. Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote the French original. Elizabeth Gilbert Martin translated it for Scribner's, who issued it in 1893. Portraits accompany the text. The introduction borrows Guizot's advice: turn to history for romance. Real courts, the author holds, outdo the historical novel. The first part covers the years 1715 to 1744.

The opening chapters stage the king's childhood betrothal. The Infanta Marie Anne Victoire was first chosen as his bride. The marriage of Marie Leczinska replaced that plan. The disgrace of the Marquise de Prie follows. One chapter is titled The King Faithful to the Queen. The volume sits among sister works on Marie Antoinette and Josephine. Court manners, favour, and intrigue are its matter throughout.
79712-last-years-of-louis-xv:
Imbert de Saint-Amand's Last Years of Louis XV, in Elizabeth Gilbert Martin's translation, was published by Scribner's at New York in 1893, with portraits. The book belongs to the Women of Versailles series. A first part surveys the court and the city at the reign's end: the king, nobility, clergy, magistracy, middle classes, people, political women, love, the famous salons, and the philosophers. The second part turns to the women of Versailles.

Chapters follow the beginnings and triumphs of the Countess Du Barry, Madame Louise as a Carmelite novice, and the childhood of Marie Antoinette. Her arrival in France, the marriage festivities, and her clash with Du Barry lead to the death of Louis the Fifteenth. An epilogue ends on Du Barry's scaffold. Saint-Amand's introduction describes his method as a kind of incarnation in the dead, learned from memoirs and daily tittle-tattle.
banbury-chap-books-and-nursery-toy-book-:
Edwin Pearson compiled this antiquarian survey of Banbury chapbooks and nursery toy books of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Over eight hundred small woodcut illustrations crowd the study, each numbered for the plain-text reader. Pearson reprints whole toy books and catalogues their cuts, printers, and variants with a collector's patience.

Samples include Dame Trot's Cat, taught, marketed, dressed, and set fighting Dog Ball in a string of cuts. A versified Robinson Crusoe follows, designed by Cruikshank: the raft, the tame goat, the footprints, the island crossed in seven pictures. Jack Sprat and his wife Joan appear from the Cruikshank school. The volume preserves the cheap print that taught Georgian children to read, and shows how the same blocks served town after town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory XV, born Alessandro Ludovisi at Bologna in January 1554, was elected on 9 February 1621 and died at Rome on 8 July 1623. Schooled by Jesuits at the Roman and German Colleges, he graduated in canon and civil law at Bologna. He served as judge of the Capitol under Gregory XIII, referendary and rota member under Clement VIII, Archbishop of Bologna in 1612, nuncio to Savoy, and cardinal in 1616.

Elected chiefly through Cardinal Borghese at sixty-seven and in bad health, his two years and five months proved remarkably active. He needed a strong, trusted helper and chose his nephew Ludovico Ludovisi, aged twenty-five. He made Ludovico cardinal on the pontificate's third day despite nepotism charges, with his brother Orazio commanding the papal army. Ludovico advanced his family but served the Church well. Gregory's bull Aeterni Patris of November 1621 limited papal elections to scrutiny, compromise, and quasi-inspiration.
